terms.gloss: money assigned (to a person or a purpose), a grant
terms.grammar: noun phrase: pecūnia, first declension, with the participle of attribuō
evidence: Cic. Phil. 14.38: ad eam rem pecūniam dare, attribuere, solvere
terms.comment: Latin says it with the verb: pecūniam alicui attribuere, to assign money to someone, of public money paid out for a purpose (Lewis & Short s.v. attribuō). A grant for one’s studies, pecūnia ad studia attribūta.

terms.gloss: a grant (paid in instalments), a stipend
evidence: M-O s.v. grant (of money, as from foundation sponsoring research), after Desfontaines (1798)
terms.comment: Classically a soldier’s pay, and a tribute paid in money by a subject people (Lewis & Short); so it suits a grant paid out regularly, like a salary, rather than a single sum.

phrases.latin: opera ex pecūniā attribūtā dīvīsāque inter sē haec fēcērunt
phrases.english: out of the money granted them and divided between them they built the following works

sources: Lewis & Short: attribuo · Lewis & Short: stipendium
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. grant (of money).
Livy and Cicero checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (11 November 2026); in Livy that edition prints [con]fēcērunt, deleting the prefix.
